---
title: "Lumbar Radicular Pain: Introduction"
---

**Radicular pain** is a type of neuropathic pain generated by irritation or inflammation of a spinal nerve root. In the lumbar spine, this often presents as low back or buttock pain that radiates down the leg. Patients may describe this pain as sudden, shooting, burning, electric, sharp, or stabbing.

Radicular pain is a high-yield clinical topic because it connects anatomy, pain physiology, neurologic examination, and imaging to determine the ideal plan for intervention. It is also commonly encountered across a variety of specialties including primary care, emergency medicine, neurology, orthopedics, neurosurgery, and of course, pain medicine.

::: {.callout-note}
## By the end of this module, you should be comfortable with:

- [ ] Defining radicular pain and distinguishing it from radiculopathy
- [ ] Explaining how disc herniation or degenerative narrowing can irritate a spinal nerve root
- [ ] Understanding traversing versus exiting nerve root involvement
- [ ] Localizing common clinical patterns by nerve root level
- [ ] Identifying red flags and knowing when investigations are useful
- [ ] Comparing conservative, interventional, and surgical management options
:::

## Case example

The following case will be used as a point of reference throughout this module:

A 24-year-old male develops sudden right-sided leg pain while deadlifting. The pain begins in the low back and radiates down the leg with a sharp, electric quality.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Pause and think

Based on the information you have so far, what features of this presentation suggest **radicular pain** rather than nonspecific low back pain?

<details>
<summary>Show answer</summary>

The key feature is **radiating leg pain** with a sharp or electric quality, which suggests irritation of a spinal nerve root. Try to think through possible causes of this pain in an otherwise healthy young patient before moving to the next section of this module. 

</details>
:::
